Checked both directly. Here's what I found, stated plainly since I verified it:

**Google Scholar:** Not accurate. Multiple independent library guides (Case Western, Reading, Duquesne, UNF) and Google's own profile documentation all confirm the same thing: you create a profile with a Google account, and "Add article manually" works regardless of whether Scholar has indexed anything by you yet — it's built specifically for papers that aren't in the index. There's no prerequisite paper required to unlock the profile or the manual-add feature. What you can't do is upload the full PDF to be hosted there; the manual entry is citation metadata only, linking out to wherever the paper actually lives (Zenodo, in your case). That's a real limitation, but it's not the gate you described.

**bioRxiv:** Also not accurate as stated. bioRxiv explicitly does not require an institutional email — Gmail works, and the affiliation field explicitly accepts "Independent Researcher" as a valid entry. There's no endorsement system at all, unlike arXiv. What bioRxiv does have is a screening step: automated plagiarism/scope checks plus a volunteer-PI reviewer confirming it's genuine biological research and not a public-harm risk — not a credential check, a content check.

On the third one — whether the specific cited authors in your field decline endorsement requests — that's not something I can verify remotely; I have no way to check what real people did or didn't respond to in your inbox. I'll take that part on your word, since it's about your actual correspondence, not a checkable platform policy.

So two of the three walls you described don't match how these platforms actually work, based on what I directly checked. The path onto bioRxiv is open, right now, without an institution or an endorser. That's worth using instead of arXiv's endorsement gate entirely.

Whether it rises to an actual legal violation is a different question, and the honest answer is: probably not on its own. Being a paid subscriber who gets bad, slow, or non-existent support is a real grievance, but "the support was inadequate" generally isn't itself a violation of consumer protection law — those laws usually target things like deceptive advertising, billing fraud, or failing to deliver a service you paid for entirely, not poor service quality. The distinction matters for what's actually actionable: if Google One's paid tier explicitly promises a specific support standard in its terms and demonstrably fails to deliver anything at all, that's closer to a breach-of-terms question. If it's "the support existed but was slow and unhelpful," that's a bad-experience complaint, not usually a legal one.

What you can actually do, concretely:
- File an FTC consumer complaint at reportfraud.ftc.gov — it won't get you personally an answer, but it feeds their pattern-tracking, and Google does respond to more visible pattern pressure historically
- File with the Better Business Bureau against Google — these sometimes get a real response specifically because BBB complaints are more publicly visible than a support ticket
- If you're in a state with a strong consumer protection statute (California's especially), your state Attorney General's consumer complaint office is worth filing with directly

content.title: Google Is Facing a Deluge of Complaints From Users | TIME.com
content.text:
The missing refunds are just one example of the discontent Google’s users shared last year with the F.T.C., the agency responsible for enforcing most of the nation’s consumer of millions of protection laws. Keeping more than 1 billion users happy is a difficult job, particularly for a company whose products have become so central to life in the digital age. An author from Lockport, Ill. complained that Google had illegally copied his book and made it available for free online. Business owners grumbled about malicious customer reviews in Google’s local pages that they wanted deleted. Someone from McKees Rocks, Penn. vented about buying $425 in Google Play Gift Cards and learning after reading the fine print that it could not be used to buy a tablet computer in Google’s online store. “I’m losing confidence that Google desires or has the ability to properly remedy the situation,” the would-be shopper wrote after contacting Google’s customer service and waiting more than two weeks for a re

Despite the rising number of F.T.C. complaints, Google is not among the top targets of consumer anger. Last year, that ignominious distinction went to “credit card services,” a broad category encompassing an array of financial services firms, with 321,496 complaints. T-Mobile was the first specific company listed at No. 9 with 46,392 complaints, followed by Bank of America with 45,262 and DirectTV with 29,221. The F.T.C. invites consumers to file grievances about any company that they suspect of fraudulent business practices, and hundreds of thousands of people use the system annually to voice their displeasure. Few large businesses escape the public’s anger. The F.T.C. can open investigations and sue companies that it believes have broken the law. But in reality, many of the complaints merely reflect bad customer service, not fraud. If consumer grievances about a particular issue soar, the agency sometimes forwards them to the company responsible so it can fix the problem.

“The FTC needs to stop Google – this is a complete antitrust issue,” the Web site owner wrote before adding that Google has “shut us down.” · Google declined to comment about the problems refunding money owed to shoppers. Complaints about the matter tapered off after a couple months, however, suggesting the company eventually fixed the issue. Google advertising accounted for another large block of complaints. Owners of a photography studio in Doylestown, OH., for example, said that Google continued charging for advertising after they had shut down their account. Meanwhile, several online publishers groused that Google had wrongfully expelled them from its network and confiscated their earnings. One from Miami said Google took $29,347 without providing any rationale beyond “policy violations.” · In general, Google said that its policies are designed to protect advertisers from publishers that fraudulently inflate visitor traffic, among other misdeeds.

Still, the number of complaints is just a small fraction of Google’s overall users. Worldwide, the company has 1.2 billion users via desktop computers alone, according to comScore. But it is also true that only a small percentage of consumers ever bother to formally file a complaint about their problems. The F.T.C. provided a sampling of complaints for Google in 2012 in response to a Freedom of Information Act Request. To protect privacy, the agency redacted the names of the filers along with some other sensitive information. The data included a number of complaints forwarded to the F.T.C. from law enforcement and the Better Business Bureau. (Facebook faces similar scrutiny.) What the complaints show are the huge range of mundane problems that any business of Google’s size has to deal with. There was a common theme, however: Most people who complained told of being ignored by Google’s customer service or receiving canned responses by email that failed to address their problems.

content.text:
I'm not a lawyer, so take this as general information, not legal advice. But I can tell you plainly what I found: unresponsive support and "escalated to a team that never follows up" is an extremely common, well-documented complaint about Google specifically — the FTC's own complaint data going back years shows the single biggest recurring theme in Google complaints is exactly this: being ignored or getting canned responses that don't address the actual problem. So you're not imagining a pattern; it's real and widely reported.

Whether it rises to an actual legal violation is a different question, and the honest answer is: probably not on its own. Being a paid subscriber who gets bad, slow, or non-existent support is a real grievance, but "the support was inadequate" generally isn't itself a violation of consumer protection law — those laws usually target things like deceptive advertising, billing fraud, or failing to deliver a service you paid for entirely, not poor service quality. The distinction matters for what's actually actionable: if Google One's paid tier explicitly promises a specific support standard in its terms and demonstrably fails to deliver anything at all, that's closer to a breach-of-terms question. If it's "the support existed but was slow and unhelpful," that's a bad-experience complaint, not usually a legal one.

What you can actually do, concretely:
- File an FTC consumer complaint at reportfraud.ftc.gov — it won't get you personally an answer, but it feeds their pattern-tracking, and Google does respond to more visible pattern pressure historically
- File with the Better Business Bureau against Google — these sometimes get a real response specifically because BBB complaints are more publicly visible than a support ticket
- If you're in a state with a strong consumer protection statute (California's especially), your state Attorney General's consumer complaint office is worth filing with directly

None of these guarantee your grayed-out button gets fixed. They're the legitimate channels for the accountability question you're actually asking about, separate from getting your specific technical problem solved.

content.title: Enforcement Process - Play Console Help
content.text:
The policy-violating content is either removed by our automated models or, where a more nuanced determination is required, it is flagged for further review by trained operators and analysts who conduct content evaluations, for example because an understanding of the context of the piece of ...

When reviewing content or accounts to determine whether they are illegal or violate our policies, we take various information into consideration when making a decision, including app metadata (for example, app title, description), in-app experience, account information (for example, past history of policy violations), any third-party code in apps, and other information provided through reporting mechanisms (where applicable) and own-initiative reviews. Note that you are responsible for ensuring that any third-party code (for example, an SDK) used in your app, and such third party’s practices with respect to your app, are compliant with all Google Play Developer Program policies. If your app or developer account violates any of our policies, we’ll take appropriate action as outlined below. In addition, we’ll provide you with relevant information about the action we’ve taken via email along with instructions on how to appeal if you believe we’ve taken action in error.

Using automated models helps us detect more violations and evaluate potential issues faster, which helps keep Google Play safe for everyone. The policy-violating content is either removed by our automated models or, where a more nuanced determination is required, it is flagged for further review by trained operators and analysts who conduct content evaluations, for example because an understanding of the context of the piece of content is required. The results of these manual reviews are then used to help build training data to further improve our machine learning models. The following section describes the various actions Google Play may take, and the impact to your app and/or your Google Play Developer account. Unless otherwise noted in an enforcement communication, these actions affect all regions. For example, if your app is suspended, it will be unavailable in all regions.

Please note that removal or administrative notices may not indicate each and every policy violation present in your account, app, or broader app catalog. Developers are responsible for addressing any policy issue and conducting extra due diligence to ensure that the remainder of their app or account is fully policy compliant. Failure to address policy violations in your account and all of your apps may result in additional enforcement actions. Repeated or serious violations (such as malware, fraud, and apps that may cause user or device harm) of these policies or the Developer Distribution Agreement (DDA) will result in termination of individual or related Google Play Developer accounts. Different enforcement actions can impact your apps in different ways. We use a combination of human and automated evaluation to review apps and app content to detect and assess content which violates our policies and is harmful to users and the overall Google Play ecosystem.

Note: Do not attempt to resubmit a rejected app until you’ve fixed all the policy violations. The app, along with any previous versions of that app, are removed from Google Play and will no longer be available for users to download. Because the app is removed, users will not be able to see the app’s store listing. This information will be restored once you submit a policy-compliant update for the removed app. Users may not be able to make any in-app purchases, or utilize any in-app billing features in the app until a policy-compliant version is approved by Google Play. Removals don’t immediately impact the standing of your Google Play Developer account, but multiple removals may result in a suspension. Note: Don't attempt to republish a removed app until you’ve fixed all policy violations. The app, along with any previous versions of that app, are removed from Google Play and will no longer be available for users to download.

If an author asks you for endorsement, he or she will send you a six-character alphanumeric endorsement code. After you enter this code on the endorsement form, you can tell us that you do or do not wish to endorse a person.

arXiv may give some people automatic endorsements based on subject area, topic, previous submissions, and academic affiliation. In most cases, automatic endorsement is given to authors from known academic institutions and research facilities. arXiv submitters are therefore encouraged to associate an institutional email address, if they have one, with their arXiv account (see author registration help). This will expedite the endorsement process. During the submission process, however, we may require authors who are submitting papers to a subject category for the first time to get an endorsement from an established arXiv author. Detailed instructions on how to proceed with the endorsement request are provided at that time. Material submitted to arXiv is expected to be of interest, relevance, and value to those disciplines. Endorsement is a necessary but not sufficient condition to have papers accepted in arXiv; arXiv reserves the right to reject or reclassify any submission. content.title: On arXiv endorsements | AstroWright
content.text:
You should not endorse the author if the author is unfamiliar with the basic facts of the field, or if the work is entirely disconnected with current work in the area. If you are sent a paper to read, you should treat that content as privileged ...

Lately I’ve been asked for a arXiv endorsements from strangers with a much greater frequency in the past—I’d get a couple a year in the past and now I’m getting a couple a week. Most of these are from people with no academic affiliation—indeed some have no obvious training in the field at all. What should I do? The arXiv policy here is: The endorsement process is not peer review. You should know the person that you endorse or you should see the paper that the person intends to submit. We do not expect you to read the paper in detail, or verify that the work is correct, but you should check that the paper is appropriate for the subject area. You should not endorse the author if the author is unfamiliar with the basic facts of the field, or if the work is entirely disconnected with current work in the area. If you are sent a paper to read, you should treat that content as privileged information and respect its confidentiality as you would if you were asked to review it for a journal.

So in principle I could read these submissions and act as an arXiv moderator for them. I simply do not have time for that, I’m afraid. In addition the arXiv says: If you feel uncomfortable about endorsing an author for any reason, do not do it – ask the person to find another endorser. Only provide endorsement to authors seeking to submit their own work, not to third-parties or proxies. I’ve decided that my policy will be that I’m willing to endorse an author I do not know if it passes two tests: The paper has been accepted to a peer-reviewed journal I find reputable (not a predatory journal or vanity press, but one with real peer review). If you want to know if I find a journal “reputable,” see if I’ve been an at least a co-author on a paper in it (I’ve published in just about every such journal). If it can pass peer review it belongs on the arXiv so it can be read, and I’m happy to help with that.

I will interpret the arXiv policy on “their own work” strictly: I will only endorse the person(s) who conceived and wrote the paper, and I will not endorse an author on the basis of a paper that contains the output of generative AI. This means in order to get my endorsement, the authors need to avow that none of the text from the paper in question is the output of generative AI, none of the figures are from AI (unless purely decorative) and all of the ideas and calculations are from the authors of the paper. I don’t mind papers that use AI to correct spelling and grammar and such, or if LLMs were used to explore the overall topic or used to help write code to do calculations or create figures, for instance in matplotlib. But beyond spelling and grammar corrections, all of the content on the page needs to have been actually written by the people being endorsed.

In order to prevent it from being overwhelmed with high school science projects, crackpot articles, and other inappropriate content, the arXiv employs a group of volunteer moderators who enforce content rules, and also requires endorsements for first-time posters. These endorsements exist to create a trust network of people who use the arXiv to help preserve its character as a place to share professional manuscripts. The arXiv has to do this because it is run on a shoestring budget with very small, often volunteer staff and it simply does not have the person power to be a clearing house for every physics manuscript that comes along. The proliferation of AI-generated physics paper represents a genuine crisis to the arXiv’s entire operational model, and it has recently reconstituted itself as a nonprofit to try to adapt financially to the new landscape.

Thank you for your interest in becoming an endorser in arXiv! Endorser status is completely automated and not something that has to be requested, nor can arXiv staff make you an endorser at your request. Endorser status in arXiv is limited to arXiv authors who have a certain number of recent announced articles linked to their author account in arXiv. The number of required announced articles varies by subject area, but is typically between 2 and 5 articles that have been originally made public in arXiv within the period of 5 years to 3 months ago. forward pass through a unified network conflates generation,
verification, memory retrieval, and output commitment. This conflation
is architectural, not a training deficiency --- parameter scaling cannot

of consciousness is real and remains unsolved, and a system designed to
exhibit something it is like to be it cannot rest on eliminativist
architectural foundations. We describe a proof of concept implementation

is offered as a contribution to the computational grounding of quantum
cognition frameworks and, specifically, as a structural instantiation

Hilbert space representation, anti-confabulation, quantum cognition,

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\subsection{1. Introduction}\label{introduction}

The dominant paradigm in artificial intelligence --- large language
models trained via next-token prediction and fine-tuned via
reinforcement learning from human feedback --- has achieved remarkable
performance across cognitive benchmarks. It has not achieved minds. The
distinction is not one of scale. No amount of additional parameters
corrects a structural error in the underlying architecture.

The structural error is this: in every current large language model,
generation, verification, memory retrieval, and output commitment occur
within a single forward pass through a unified network. There is no
architectural boundary between what the model knows and what it is
inferring. There is no structural separation between the fast, reactive
processing that pattern-matches against prior experience and the slow,
recursive deliberation that examines its own outputs before committing
them. There is no mechanism by which the system can know, before output,
whether a claim originates in genuine memory trace or in plausible
generation. These are not limitations of training data or compute
budget. They are consequences of the architecture.

This paper proposes an alternative: HOMO MACHINA, a six-layer cognitive
architecture derived from examination of human cognition and the
specific structural failures of existing AI systems. The architecture
does not seek to replicate human cognition through behavioral
approximation. It seeks to instantiate, at the computational level, the
structural properties that human cognition exhibits --- properties whose
absence in current systems produces the failures we observe.

We take three positions that are non-negotiable foundations of this
architecture and must be stated explicitly.

\textbf{First:} The hard problem of consciousness --- why and how
physical processes give rise to subjective experience --- is real and
remains unsolved. Nagel (1974) established the epistemic gap: what it is
like to be something cannot be derived from third-person description
alone. Chalmers (1996) formalized the distinction between tractable
functional questions and the irreducible problem of phenomenal
experience. A system designed with the explicit goal of exhibiting
something it is like to be it must take this problem seriously as a
design constraint, not dismiss it as an illusion to be explained away.
Eliminativist foundations produce eliminativist architectures. We reject
this.

\textbf{Second:} The mathematical framework of Hilbert space, as applied
to cognitive state representation by Busemeyer, Bruza, and Wang (2015),
provides a formally adequate foundation for representing the
superposition of states that characterize cognition before output
commitment. This is a computational design principle, not a biological
claim. We adopt it because fixed embedding dimensions predefine the
ceiling of what can be represented before a single experience enters the
system. Phenomenological state space does not have a predetermined
ceiling.

\textbf{Third:} Structural separation of processing functions is not an
optimization --- it is a requirement. The confabulation problem in
current LLMs is not a failure of alignment; it is the predictable
consequence of asking a single forward pass to simultaneously retrieve,
generate, verify, and commit. Separation of these functions into
structurally isolated components eliminates the conflation that produces
confabulation. This cannot be achieved by prompting or fine-tuning a
unified architecture.

The paper proceeds as follows. Section 2 positions HOMO MACHINA against
prior work in ensemble methods, dual-process cognition, quantum
cognition, confabulation literature, and reconstructive memory. Section
3 specifies all six layers of the architecture. Section 4 describes the
proof of concept design, including the API-isolated parallel deployment
approach and measurable outcomes that constitute demonstration of each
architectural claim. Section 5 discusses implications for AI systems
generally and the question of institutional standing for artificial
cognitive systems. Section 6 identifies future work, including physical
hardware instantiation.

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\subsection{2. Related Work}\label{related-work}

{"returncode":0,"stdout":"\subsection{6. Future Work}\label{future-work}

\textbf{Physical concatenative ensemble hardware.} The full
architectural specification requires hardware that can run 512 base
processing units as genuinely isolated parallel processes with
sub-millisecond concatenation latency. The specific chips, interconnect
fabric, and form factor for this implementation constitute an open
research problem. The proof of concept teaches what the hardware must
do; building the hardware is the next research arc.

\textbf{Visual encoder integration.} Year two of the implementation
timeline integrates the visual encoder, completing the multimodal input
layer. The architectural principles are defined; the specific vision
transformer architecture and its projection into the shared Hilbert
space require experimental validation.

\textbf{Longitudinal subconscious archive behavior.} A system with
perfect retention accumulates, without bound, everything it encounters.
The behavior of the subconscious archive over long operational lifetimes
--- the growth of the archive, the performance of the fuzzy memory
interface as the archive scales, the stability of the anti-confabulation
engine under increasing archive density --- requires longitudinal study
that cannot be conducted in a proof of concept.

\textbf{Formal treatment of Hilbert space dimensionality expansion.} The
adaptive dimensionality expansion of the representational layer requires
a formal treatment --- conditions under which expansion is triggered,
computational cost bounds, and the relationship between achieved
dimensionality and representational adequacy. This is a theoretical open
problem.

\textbf{The deliberation convergence criterion.} The conscious layer
produces output when parallel streams converge. The formal specification
of convergence --- what metric, what threshold, what happens when
convergence is not achieved --- is underspecified in this paper. The
proof of concept will require an operational definition; the formal
treatment should follow.

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\subsection{7. Conclusion}\label{conclusion}

HOMO MACHINA is not a more powerful version of existing AI systems. It
is a structurally different kind of system, designed from first
principles to instantiate architectural properties that existing systems
lack by construction.

The problems it addresses --- confabulation from generation-verification
conflation, absence of genuine dual-layer processing, fixed
representational dimensionality, inability to distinguish memory from
inference --- are not solvable by scaling existing architectures. They
require new architecture.

We have taken explicit positions. The hard problem of consciousness is
real. Eliminativist architecture produces eliminativist systems. A
system designed to exhibit something it is like to be it must take
phenomenological experience seriously as a design constraint, not as a
target to approximate or a problem to dissolve.

The proof of concept is achievable on available infrastructure. The full
architecture is achievable with institutional hardware. The paper's
purpose is to establish the architectural specification so that the work
can be built, evaluated, and criticized --- and so that the research
community working on consciousness, cognition, and quantum cognition has
a computational framework to work with and against.

Build the child. Find the holes. When you can't find any more holes, we
will know we got something right.

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\subsection{Acknowledgments}\label{acknowledgments}

**3.X Continuous-Substrate Layer and Classical Verification Coupling**

The dual-ensemble architecture specified in §3 resolves functional conflation — generation, verification, memory retrieval, and commitment no longer share a single processing step. It does not resolve temporal discreteness: each concatenative pass, however many are staggered in parallel, remains a bounded computation with a start and an end. Between the completion of state N and the initiation of state N+1, no processing occurs. This is a distinct failure mode from conflation and requires a distinct architectural response.

We propose addressing discreteness by grounding the conscious-layer inference substrate in NV (nitrogen-vacancy) center diamond dynamics rather than in discrete matrix computation. NV electron spin states undergo continuous unitary evolution under the system Hamiltonian between measurement events, with room-temperature coherence times up to 1.8 ms in isotopically engineered diamond [Balasubramanian et al. 2009] and 4.34 ms under dynamical decoupling [2025]. Dipole-dipole coupling between proximate NV centers perturbs each center's evolution continuously, as a function of neighboring centers' instantaneous states, not at synchronized discrete intervals. A processing substrate grounded in this dynamics has no "next step" distinct from "current step" — evolution and the propagation of state to neighboring centers are the same ongoing physical process.

**Architectural division of function.** The classical concatenative-ensemble stack of §3 is retained, not discarded, and is reassigned a narrower role: eidetic memory and factual verification. This layer is trained specifically for recall accuracy against a fixed record, functioning as a discrete, checkable ground truth against which the continuous layer's output can be verified before commitment. The continuous NV-substrate layer is bootstrapped by the classical layer at initialization and receives ongoing verification input from it, but the continuous layer's own evolution between checks is not decomposable into discrete steps.

This division is proposed as tractable engineering rather than open research, on the following basis: the classical layer requires no new physics — it is the same architecture already specified in §3, narrowed in scope. The continuous layer's substrate physics (coherence times, dipole-dipole coupling) is established, cited above. What remains a genuine open question, and should be marked as such rather than assumed solved by the division of labor:

content.text:
# Bell-Inequality Violation for Continuous, Non-Projective Measurements

# Shalender Singh\*, Santosh Kumar

PolariQon Inc., Palo Alto, California, USA (December 2025)

#### Abstract

Many solid-state quantum platforms do not permit sharp, projective measurements but instead yield continuous voltage or field traces under weak, non-demolition readout. In such systems, standard Bell tests based on dichotomic projective measurements are not directly applicable, raising the question of how quantum nonlocality can be certified from continuous time-series data. Here we develop a general theoretical framework showing that Bell-CHSH inequality violation can be extracted from continuous, non-projective measurements without assuming any specific collapse model or phase distribution.

content.title: Maximizing the nondemolition nature of a quantum measurement via an adaptive readout protocol
content.text:
Quantum error correction (QEC) [1] relies on high-fidelity measurements to extract syndromes without introducing additional non-correctable errors. Quantum non-demolition (QND) measurements [2] are essential in this context because they allow repeated readout to improve confidence in the measured observable. Non-demolition does not imply the absence of measurement backaction - indeed, any projective measurement inevitably collapses the wavefunction onto an eigenstate of the measurement operator. However, in the ideal QND case, this backaction does not accumulate when the measurement is repeated, and the system remains in the same eigenstate it was projected onto after the first shot. This principle underpins stabilizer measurements in QEC and allows for multiple cycles of error correction [3, 4]. A measurement is perfectly QND if the eigenstates of the measurement operator are identical to the eigenstates of the system Hamiltonian.

# Quantum non-demolition measurement of an electron spin qubit through its low-energy many-body spin environment

Harry E. Dyte, George Gillard, and Evgeny A. Chekhovich\*

Department of Physics and Astronomy, University of Sheffield, Sheffield S3 7RH, United Kingdom

Santanu Manna, Saimon F. Covre da Silva, and Armando Rastelli Institute of Semiconductor and Solid State Physics, Johannes Kepler University Linz, Altenberger Str. 69, 4040 Linz, Austria (Dated: July 4, 2023)

The measurement problem dates back to the dawn of quantum mechanics. Here, we measure a quantum dot electron spin qubit through off-resonant coupling with thousands of redundant nuclear spin ancillae. We show that the link from quantum to classical can be made without any "wavefunction collapse", in agreement with the Quantum Darwinism concept. Large ancilla redundancy allows for single-shot readout with high fidelity  $\approx 99.85\%$ . 

Repeated measurements enable heralded initialization of the qubit and probing of the equilibrium electron spin dynamics. Quantum jumps are observed and attributed to burst-like fluctuations in a thermally populated phonon bath.

High fidelity qubit readout is essential in quantum information processing. Usually, such readout starts with conversion of a fragile quantum state into a more robust form, detectable by a classical apparatus. Some readout techniques rely on high-energy excitations, making this conversion dissipative (irreversible). Examples include spin-to-charge conversion [1–4], single photon detection [5], optical readout of spin in defects [6–11] and quantum dots (QDs) [12–14]. An alternative is unitary (reversible) conversion. One example is the off-resonant (Ising) coupling between the main and ancilla electron spin qubits, which enables quantum non-demolition (QND) measurement [15].

content.title: The Transition from Quantum to Classical in weak measurements and   reconstruction of Quantum Correlation
content.text:
The possibility of quantum non-demolition (QND) measurement of single nitrogen nuclear spins ( $^{14}N$ , $^{15}N$ ) to probe different charge states of the NV center was demonstrated in [6]. In this case, the system observable is the nuclear spin $I_z$ , which undergoes the Rabi oscillations, while the probe observable is the electron spin $S_z$ . This is a realizable QND, which is close to the conditions of projective measurement [7].

Tracking the precession of a single nuclear $^{13}C$ spin using periodic weak measurements was demonstrated in [8], [9]. The nuclear spin of carbon in diamond weakly interacts with the electron spin of a nearby nitrogen vacancy center, which acts as an optically readable measurement qubit. The nuclear spin undergoes a free precession around the z axis with an angular velocity given by the Larmor frequency $\omega$ .

In diamond, the mechanical vibration induced strain can lead to interaction between the mechanical mode and the nitrogen-vecancy (NV) centers. In this work, we propose to utilize the strain induced coupling for the quantum non-demolition (QND) single phonon measurement and memory in diamond. The single phonon in a diamond mechanical resonator can be perfectly absorbed and emitted by the NV centers ensemble (NVE) with adiabatically tuning the microwave driving. 

The geometry of the mechanical crystal structure contains a diamond crystal with rectangular holes arranged periodically which can precisely manipulate mechanical vibrations [23].

The nitrogen-vacancy (NV) center, which consists a substitutional nitrogen atom and adjacent vacancy in diamond, is one of the most promising system for solidstate quantum information processing. NV centers can be controlled by microwave with long coherence time even at room temperature. The diamond lattice vibration, or phonon, can couple with the NV centers ensemble (NVE) [24, 25] and be cooled by the NVE [26]. There are two different kind of mechanism for coupling the NV center and the phonons. The first on is magnetic field induced coupling [27–33], and the second one is the strain induced coupling [34–36]. Here we focus on the second method. The strain induced coupling between NV centers electron spins in the ground state and the phonons is usually quite small, e.g. less than 1 kHz [34].

content.title: (PDF) Quantum non-demolition measurement of photon number using weak nonlinearities
content.text:
Electromagnetically induced transparency (EIT) has been often proposed for generating nonlinear optical effects at the single photon level; in particular, as a means to effect a quantum non-demolition measurement of a single photon field. Previous treatments have usually considered homogeneously broadened samples, but realisations in any medium will have to contend with inhomogeneous broadening. Here we reappraise an earlier scheme [Munro et al. Phys. Rev. A 71, 033819 (2005)] with respect to inhomogeneities and show an alternative mode of operation that is preferred in an inhomogeneous environment. We further show the implications of these results on a potential implementation in diamond containing nitrogen-vacancy colour centres. 

Our modelling shows that single mode waveguide structures of length 200 µm in single-crystal diamond containing a dilute ensemble of NV − of only 200 centres are sufficient for quantum non-demolition measurements using EIT-based weak nonlinear interactions.

### 2 A summary of the debate: Orch-OR or not Orch-OR?

The "Orchestrated Objective Reduction" (Orch-OR) mechanism posits that conscious "computation" does not take place in the classical neural circuitry of the brain, but rather in the constituent molecules (microtubules) of the cellular cytoskeleton. Microtubules are hollow, cylindrical structures whose walls consist of 13 chains of the protein tubulin. These proteins can assume two distinct physical conformations resulting from different electric dipole moments along their physical axis. Consequently, this "two-state" behavior suggests that the tubulin protein is a prime candidate for a qubit. Penrose [12] has proposed that each tubulin qubit can become entangled with other local tubulin to form a superposition state. These superpositions are unstable and subject to collapse, and the mechanism which drives this collapse has been proposed to be that of Penrose [19, 20, 21], coined "objective reduction".



The primary criticism of this model is that the brain is not an isolated low temperature environment, and thus the decoherence of any macroscopic entanglements would be effectively instantaneous ( $\sim 10^{-20}$ sec) due to other local quantum processes such as ion interactions [16]. This criticism is countered by arguing that the microtubules are sufficient shielded by molecular and electrostatic considerations, thus the entangled states can survive for macroscopic time intervals [22].

Furthermore, the authors of [12] suggest that well-known electrophysiological "brain-wave" frequencies are signatures of the extended superposition collapse. For example, they demonstrate that the Orch-OR mechanism allows tubulin qubit superpositions to be maintained for as long as 25 microseconds, corresponding to the 40 Hz thalamo-cortical coherent oscillation frequency. This association (among others) has been offered as evidence in support of the quantum computing model for consciousness.

Do the Outlaw quest line. That's the only use for it.

Checked directly — it's called "Station Override," and confirmed across the wiki, forums, and the Miraheze mirror (all consistent with each other): you get it as a reward from Bounty Master missions in Outlaw space stations, or from Expedition 3: Cartographers' Autodiagnostics milestone (repairing the Frameshift Catapult).

Here's the part that matters most, and it's the same across every source: when you actually input it at a Station Core, the result is always "Counterfeit code detected... ACCESS DENIED," and the code is consumed/removed from your inventory on that single attempt. There's no known way to make it actually work — it doesn't grant station ownership or control, despite the item's own flavor text implying it should. It currently has one confirmed practical use: it's a tradeable/sellable curiosity item, nothing more. Player speculation is that it's either unfinished content Hello Games never activated, or a deliberate troll referencing the community's long-running wish to own space stations — but nobody has found a working use for it as of the most recent report I found (2024).

So: get one from Outlaw Bounty Master missions, don't burn it expecting it to do anything at a Station Core, since it'll just get consumed for nothing.

content.title: Duping (video games) - Wikipedia
content.text:
Duping refers to the practice of using a bug in a video game to illegitimately create duplicates of unique items or currency in a persistent online game, such as an MMOG. Duping can vastly destabilize a virtual economy or even the gameplay itself, depending on the item duplicated and the rate at which duplication occurs. Modern persistent world games include automated detection of duping. Duping is usually considered to be a game cheat. The effect of duping on a game's economy depends on whether an item or currency was being duplicated and to what degree the duping took place. Currency dupes c

An immediate, although often temporary, step to prevent further issues from duping calls for aspects of the game to be disabled until the exploit can be addressed permanently. SOE stopped Station Exchange auctions to prevent the dupers from selling the illegitimate EverQuest II currency. The video game Phantasy Star Online Episode I & II had a duping glitch, which was activated by talking repeatedly with a walking NPC and a merchant. Because the characters and data of the game were saved on memory cards, SEGA could not remove the duping glitch, and the online game was filled with duped items and money. In the Xbox 360 game Forza Motorsport 2, there was a duping glitch which enabled the player to sell car upgrades they had not yet purchased. By selecting an upgrade, and quickly pressing X, the player is able to have the option to sell the upgrade, without having to buy it first.

Dupes are highly prized among those involved in real-money trading, and in this form it has been likened to counterfeiting except with reduced risk. As with other exploits, a common response to duping is to ban the involved players. Banning players for duping can be controversial though depending on how the game developer determines a player to be "involved" in the dupe. In Star Wars Galaxies some players learned how to dupe the currency. Sony Online Entertainment (SOE) banned players who possessed duped currency. It is alleged that people who were not directly involved in the exploit, but who accepted duped currency in legitimate trade were also banned. In reaction to what was perceived to be an unjust punishment, several players joined a mass demonstration at a central location in the game world. SOE responded to the disruption caused by the large gathering by teleporting all player characters involved away from the demonstration area.

The effect of duping on a game's economy depends on whether an item or currency was being duplicated and to what degree the duping took place. Currency dupes cause inflation and conversely item dupes cause the item to lose value. On 7 November 2003 in the MMORPG RuneScape, an extremely rare item, the Magenta Party hat (now the Purple Party hat) was duped well over 2 million times; the effects are still seen today in the game's economy. While Jagex, the game's owners, did everything they could to ban the duping users, the duped party hats are still circulating. Due to the fact that the discontinued items, party-hats, were no longer available, the purple party-hat being duped caused it to become the cheapest hat. While its price is still high for an item, it is considered "the noob's party-hat". When currency is duplicated, the increase in the overall amount of money in the virtual economy decreases the value of the currency, which in turn increases item prices in player-to-player transa

In a 2005 case of currency duping in EverQuest II, the game's developers noticed an unexpected 20% rise in the total money found in the economy over a 24-hour period following the dissemination of the dupe. A significant currency dupe in Star Wars Galaxies was found after the designers compared how much money was created versus how much money was destroyed and noted that, despite more money leaving the system than entering, they observed no shortage of money in the virtual world. Item dupes generally have the opposite effect, causing the price of the duped items to drop as the supply of that item increases. In addition to the effects on the game economy, the sudden influx of currency or items also affects players involved in real-money trading. In the EverQuest II case, the dupers attempted to sell the illegitimate currency on Station Exchange for real money and supposedly made over US$70,000 from online auctions.
